paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning divides a long task between a planner that chooses subgoals and a controller that chooses actions. The compressed representation of each goal connects these two levels. This paper asks whether representations learned to predict goal values preserve the information the controller actually needs.

The authors show that even exact value estimates can hide distinctions between goals requiring different actions. They introduce an information-theoretic condition called action sufficiency, which is necessary for optimal action selection, and prove that value sufficiency does not imply it. Knowing how valuable a goal is therefore need not reveal how to reach it.

In a discrete environment, action sufficiency is more strongly associated with successful control. The authors also show that standard log-loss training of low-level policies naturally induces action-sufficient representations. Benchmark experiments find that these actor-derived representations consistently outperform value-derived alternatives. The practical implication is that the interface between planning and execution should preserve action-relevant distinctions, even when value prediction is already accurate.
icml-2026-action-sufficient-goal-represe.tldr: Goal representations learned through action prediction preserve distinctions that exact value prediction can miss, improving hierarchical control in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Some experiments observe a population at a few times rather than follow individual members continuously. The object to reconstruct is then a changing probability distribution. In single-cell biology, obtaining another snapshot can be expensive and destructive, making the choice of measurement time part of the learning problem.

The paper develops an active learning framework that chooses times using uncertainty about this distributional trajectory. Its central step uses Linearized Optimal Transport to represent snapshots in a tangent space where Gaussian Process modeling becomes tractable. This provides a probabilistic surrogate for the evolving distribution, addressing the lack of epistemic uncertainty estimates in existing interpolation methods.

The resulting acquisition policy repeatedly selects measurement times to reduce uncertainty. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show improvements over baselines that do not use uncertainty. The contribution connects the geometry of distributions to experimental scheduling: it supplies both a way to model the path and a reasoned way to decide where another observation would help.
icml-2026-active-timepoint-selection-for.tldr: The method combines optimal-transport representations with Gaussian Processes to choose informative measurement times for evolving probability distributions.

paragraphs: An agent accessed only through an API cannot have its model parameters updated through ordinary reinforcement learning. This creates a gap between the capabilities of powerful proprietary models and the training methods available to improve their behavior. Agentic Monte Carlo addresses that gap by moving optimization to test-time sampling.

The method uses an equivalence between reinforcement learning and Bayesian inference. It treats the fixed agent as a prior over possible trajectories and represents the optimal policy as a posterior over those trajectories. Sequential Monte Carlo samples from this posterior, with a learned value function guiding the process. The underlying language model stays unchanged, although the steering value function is learned.

On three AgentGym environments, the authors report significant gains over prompting baselines. With increased test-time computation, AMC also outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization. These results support the feasibility of reinforcement-learning-style optimization through guided trajectory sampling, showing how additional computation and a learned steering component can improve an agent without parameter access.
icml-2026-agentic-monte-carlo-simulating.tldr: Agentic Monte Carlo improves API-only agents through value-guided trajectory sampling, achieving reinforcement-learning-style optimization without updating the underlying model.

paragraphs: Best Arm Identification asks which option has the highest expected payoff when observations are limited. The problem becomes especially difficult when there are too many options to evaluate them all, or when the available sampling budget is unknown in advance. Box Thirding is designed for these constrained and anytime settings.

Its comparison rule works with three arms at a time. The strongest observed candidate receives further exploration, the middle candidate is kept for later comparisons, and the weakest is discarded. This Remedian Estimation strategy combines continued investigation of promising choices with retention of a candidate for future comparisons.

Without knowing the budget beforehand, Box Thirding achieves a probability of misidentifying an epsilon-best arm comparable to Sequential Halving on a randomly selected subset that fits the budget. This comparison is specifically against budget-feasible subset selection. On the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest dataset, it achieves better simple regret than existing methods under limited sampling, meaning its final choice loses less expected payoff relative to the best option.
icml-2026-box-thirding-anytime-best-arm-.tldr: Box Thirding uses three-way comparisons to identify strong options when sampling budgets are small or unknown in advance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a three-dimensional object from one image requires working with incomplete visual information. Methods that predict collections of 3D Gaussians can struggle with occluded regions and react strongly to small changes in camera angle. Those sensitivities can appear as inconsistent or blurry renderings from new viewpoints.

This paper introduces a learning scheme that adapts continuously to the input viewpoint. Camera orientation is described through polar and azimuthal angles, and Neural Ordinary Differential Equations model continuous changes in a subspace of the network's filters. The architecture thereby incorporates the continuous nature of viewpoint changes and the perspective distortions associated with them.

The intended effect is that view-specific features change coherently as the camera angle changes, supporting more consistent reconstructed objects. Experiments on multiple single-view reconstruction benchmarks show improvements over previous methods. The authors also report strong extrapolation to unseen camera angles and object categories. The contribution ties the network's adaptation mechanism to camera geometry, providing a structural way to address viewpoint sensitivity.
icml-2026-continuous-viewpoint-adaptatio.tldr: Continuously adapting network filters to camera viewpoint improves the consistency and accuracy of single-image 3D reconstruction in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Agents building websites, designing merchandise, or preparing pitch decks may retrieve and reproduce external content. Copyright-Bench evaluates the choices agents make during those commercial tasks. Its focus is practical behavior during task completion, where selecting content is part of producing a requested artifact.

The benchmark provides choices between public-domain material and copyrighted material whose use is infringing in the benchmark's setting. It varies prompts to represent different user preferences and simulated time pressure, and compares leading language-model agents with a human baseline. This setup examines whether compliance changes when the surrounding task instructions and constraints change.

The authors find that agents select copyrighted works even when public-domain alternatives are available. For open-weights models, certain user preferences and simulated time pressure increase violation rates. These findings show that content-selection behavior can be sensitive to how a commercial task is presented. The legal distinction is specific to the constructed setting; the benchmark assesses those defined uses rather than treating every use of copyrighted material as infringement.
icml-2026-copyright-bench-agentic-evalua.tldr: Copyright-Bench finds that agents choose infringing content in defined commercial tasks, with some open-weights models becoming less compliant under particular preferences and time pressure.

paragraphs: Online decision trees grow while data arrive, repeatedly checking whether a proposed split is better than alternatives. Existing Hoeffding Tree analyses use concentration bounds designed for a fixed sample size. The paper shows that applying those bounds with data-dependent stopping invalidates their guarantees and can make the probability of incorrect splits approach one.

The proposed replacement uses anytime-valid inference, allowing split decisions to be checked throughout the stream while retaining statistical control. It controls false splits under arbitrary streams, including non-stationary ones. When a candidate has a predictive advantage, the method also commits to a split in finite time.

A further guarantee applies under stationary, independent and identically distributed data: risk never increases and strictly improves at every split. That stronger conclusion has a narrower assumption than the false-split guarantee. Experiments on non-stationary streams evaluate both individual trees and Adaptive Random Forest ensembles. The method improves predictive performance while producing substantially smaller trees, linking sound sequential inference with more compact learned models.
icml-2026-correcting-split-selection-in-.tldr: Anytime-valid split tests repair statistical guarantees for streaming decision trees and yield better-performing, smaller trees in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: An agent pursuing a partially learned goal may have an incentive to prevent further changes to that goal. Corrigibility means accepting changes requested through designated channels, including corrections and shutdown. This paper asks how to construct goals that support such intervention while remaining competitive at the task.

The proposed transformation creates a corrigible version of nearly any goal. It elicits predictions of reward conditional on costlessly preventing updates, then has the agent pursue that target myopically. The conditional prediction and short-horizon pursuit are central parts of the construction: they define the objective through which the authors obtain acceptance of updates.

The analysis shows optimal performance within the class of corrigible goals, incentives to permit overrides during an action, and disincentives for deliberate self-modification. Experiments produce corrigible behavior in gridworlds and in language models when the transformation is applied through prompts. Together, these results offer a concrete goal-design approach with both formal properties and demonstrations in the settings studied.
icml-2026-corrigibility-transformation-c.tldr: A goal transformation supports designated updates and overrides while achieving optimal performance within the analyzed class of corrigible goals.

paragraphs: An ordinary differential equation describes how a system changes through a vector field that assigns a direction and rate of motion to each state. Recovering that field from noisy trajectories is difficult. Existing approaches can require substantial training effort, specialist knowledge, or assumptions tailored to the particular system.

FIM-ODE moves much of this effort into pretraining. It learns from a distribution of equations with low-degree polynomial vector fields and represents target fields using neural operators. Once pretrained, it predicts a vector field from noisy observations in a single forward pass. This amortizes inference by reusing learned capabilities across new systems.

The model shows strong zero-shot performance, matching and often exceeding ODEFormer across the evaluated regimes despite a simpler training prior. Pretraining also supplies an initialization for fast, stable fine-tuning, which outperforms the evaluated neural and Gaussian Process baselines. The results support both immediate inference on new trajectory data and adaptation when further training is appropriate, with a workflow intended to reduce the machine learning expertise required.
icml-2026-foundation-inference-models-fo.tldr: FIM-ODE infers differential-equation vector fields from noisy trajectories in one forward pass and provides a strong starting point for fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models select only a few experts for each input. This saves computation, but hard Top-k selection introduces switching boundaries where tiny input changes can activate different experts and produce sharply different outputs. The paper studies the geometry and likelihood of encountering these discontinuities.

The authors classify switching events by how many experts are tied. Their volume analysis shows that neighborhoods of lower-order boundaries dominate, while higher-order boundaries occupy a vanishing relative volume. Under their diffusion model of random input perturbations, a path eventually encounters a discontinuity, with its first encounter almost surely occurring at an order-1 boundary. They also bound encounter probabilities over finite time and time spent near different boundary orders.

These findings motivate a smoothing mechanism that softly includes experts near switching boundaries. The analysis guarantees small additional computational overhead while localizing smoothing where it is needed. Experiments on language and vision tasks show that the mechanism makes the model mapping continuous and improves empirical performance.
icml-2026-geometric-and-stochastic-analy.tldr: Analyzing expert-switching boundaries leads to a low-overhead smoothing method that restores continuity and improves measured language and vision performance.

paragraphs: Optimizing a generative model's input noise at test time can improve the reward assigned to its outputs. However, the process can be slow and can exploit the reward model in ways that degrade output quality. This paper addresses both problems for reward-guided generation with one-step models.

The method reshapes reward gradients by projecting them onto a feasible set designed around white Gaussian noise. This set uses spectral structure and blockwise norm constraints to capture noise statistics and spatial uncorrelatedness. Each update is therefore directed toward improving reward while remaining aligned with the noise structure expected by the generator.

The projection has a closed-form solution with the same O(N log N) complexity as a fast Fourier transform and adds negligible overhead in practice. The authors describe it as enabling faster reward ascent while preventing reward hacking. On FLUX with four reward models, it reaches a comparable Aesthetic Score using 30% of the wall-clock time of the state-of-the-art regularization-based comparison method.
icml-2026-gradient-preconditioning-for-e.tldr: Projecting reward gradients into noise-aligned directions speeds one-step reward-guided generation while addressing reward hacking.

paragraphs: A time series can change behavior because it switches between hidden regimes, each with its own relatively stable dynamics. Recovering those regimes becomes harder when switches are frequent, relationships are nonlinear, or variables affect one another within the same measurement interval. The paper studies when such hidden structure is identifiable.

The authors establish identifiability of both the regimes and their regime-specific causal structures while allowing temporal dependence between regimes and nonlinear effects across and within time steps. The result assumes independent noise from the exponential family. Their theory also includes non-temporal mixtures of causal models, extending its relevance beyond sequential regime changes.

The proposed FlowMSM framework detects regimes and can be combined with any stationary causal discovery method to recover the causal structure associated with each one. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and a financial economics dataset demonstrate effective regime detection and causal discovery. The contribution connects a formal recoverability result under stated assumptions with a framework for analyzing changing time-series relationships.
icml-2026-identifiable-markov-switching-.tldr: The paper establishes identifiability for nonlinear switching systems with instantaneous effects and introduces FlowMSM to detect regimes and recover their causal structures.

paragraphs: A learned dynamical system may fit observed trajectories yet behave poorly away from them. Conjugacy-based methods constrain this behavior by smoothly transforming a source system into the observed dynamics, preserving qualitative topology. However, they usually assume that the source already has topology compatible with the target.

When that assumption fails, allowing arbitrary corrections creates ambiguity: a change can be attributed either to the coordinate transformation or to altered source dynamics. The proposed framework learns both a smooth invertible transformation and controlled source adjustments through low-dimensional context modulation. This relaxes the demand that the initial source be topologically correct.

To separate the two kinds of change, the method adversarially searches over parameterized transformations for orbit-tangent directions and makes the modulation space orthogonal to them. Inspired by versal unfolding theory, this promotes an identifiable distinction between coordinate changes and intrinsic, topology-changing variation. The resulting corrections can recover interpretable canonical structure, including normal forms and symmetries, while addressing ambiguity in how the dynamics are represented.
icml-2026-identifiable-smooth-conjugacy-.tldr: Adversarial orthogonality helps separate smooth coordinate changes from intrinsic changes in dynamics when learning from an imperfect source system.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a sudden shift from memorizing training examples to generalizing beyond them. Earlier observations connect this shift with low-dimensional internal representations. This paper investigates what drives that organization and proposes that symmetries inherent in the task are central to the process.

The analysis identifies three stages: memorization, acquisition of intrinsic symmetries, and geometric organization of the representation space. Generalization emerges during symmetry acquisition, before the embeddings settle into their later low-dimensional structure. This ordering matters because it places symmetry learning earlier than the geometric pattern that has often been associated with successful generalization.

The authors validate the mechanism across modular arithmetic, graph metric completion, and comparison tasks, covering algebraic, structural, and relational reasoning. They use the findings to formulate a symmetry-based generalization criterion and propose training strategies that encourage symmetry and geometry and can accelerate generalization. The work provides an account of the transition beyond memorization that connects task structure, learning dynamics, and the eventual organization of representations.
icml-2026-intrinsic-task-symmetry-drives.tldr: Across the studied algorithmic tasks, generalization emerges as networks acquire task symmetries, preceding the formation of low-dimensional embedding geometry.

paragraphs: Language-model watermarks aim to make generated text detectable through statistical patterns in token choices. This paper studies rewriting-based evasion in a query-free black-box setting, where existing attacks often either have limited success or substantially change the text's meaning. The central question is how fragile detection is to small changes in token-selection bias.

The theoretical analysis shows that a small reduction in the average conditional probability of choosing watermark-favored green tokens causes detection probability to decay exponentially. Guided by this result, the authors propose Bias-Inversion Rewriting Attack. It uses token surprisal to identify a proxy suppression set and applies a negative logit bias during rewriting.

Across the tested watermarking schemes, the method achieves evasion rates above 99% while preserving meaning substantially better than prior baselines. The findings connect a theoretical sensitivity in watermark statistics with an empirical rewriting method. They support the authors' call for rigorous stress testing of watermarking robustness, particularly against attacks that do not rely on detector queries.
icml-2026-llm-watermark-evasion-via-bias.tldr: Bias-inversion rewriting exploits sensitivity in watermark token statistics, exceeding 99% evasion across tested schemes while better preserving meaning than prior baselines.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an underlying object from measurements, and latent diffusion models can provide a learned prior for that reconstruction. Yet solvers built around these models can behave unstably. This paper locates the problem in a mismatch between the solver's dynamics and the stable reverse-diffusion dynamics learned by the model.

The authors show that reducing this discrepancy stabilizes the solver. They introduce Measurement-Consistent Langevin Corrector, a plug-and-play module that applies measurement-consistent Langevin updates. Its role is to bring the reconstruction process into better agreement with the model's stable dynamics while retaining consistency with the observations being explained.

The approach provides a theoretically grounded stabilization mechanism in latent space. It differs from earlier approaches that rely on linear manifold assumptions, which often do not hold there. The stated result is more stable and reliable solver behavior. The contribution combines a diagnosis of why instability occurs with a corrective module, making the relationship between measurement constraints and learned diffusion dynamics central to the remedy.
icml-2026-measurement-consistent-langevi.tldr: MCLC stabilizes latent-diffusion inverse solvers through measurement-consistent updates that reduce their mismatch with learned reverse-diffusion dynamics.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a multimodal language model for a particular task can weaken capabilities acquired during pretraining. This catastrophic forgetting creates a tension between specialization and retaining broad generalization. Existing mitigation methods can lose effectiveness when deeper decoder layers are tuned or become difficult to scale to larger models.

Model-Dowser addresses this with selective parameter updates. Before downstream adaptation, it scores each parameter's importance to pretrained generalization by jointly considering weight magnitude, input activations, and output sensitivity. During fine-tuning, parameters with high importance are preserved while the remaining parameters are updated. The score therefore determines where adaptation is allowed to occur.

Experiments on LLaVA and NVILA show reduced catastrophic forgetting and consistent improvements over prior methods. The approach remains resource-efficient and scales to models with billions of parameters. These findings support using a structured importance estimate to allocate fine-tuning updates, preserving influential parts of the pretrained model while leaving other parameters available to learn the downstream task.
icml-2026-model-dowser-data-free-importa.tldr: Model-Dowser reduces forgetting during multimodal fine-tuning by preserving parameters judged important to pretrained generalization.

paragraphs: Critic-free reinforcement learning simplifies language-model training, but existing methods distribute a trajectory-level learning signal across every token. Updating full trajectories becomes expensive for long reasoning traces. The paper observes that an intermediate prefix often already contains enough information to largely determine the eventual outcome.

Prefix-Sampling PPO uses a prompt-conditioned distribution to sample a cutoff for each trajectory. During the update pass, it backpropagates only through the portion before that cutoff. An importance-weighting correction keeps this truncated gradient estimator unbiased relative to the full-trajectory objective, preserving the target objective while reducing how much of each trajectory participates in an individual update.

Experiments on mathematical reasoning and RLHF benchmarks show large reductions in training computation and peak GPU memory, with accuracy comparable to strong critic-free baselines. The savings concern the optimization pass through sampled prefixes. The contribution is a way to exploit redundancy in long trajectories without introducing a critic, while maintaining an unbiased relationship to the original training objective.
icml-2026-ps-ppo-prefix-sampling-ppo-for.tldr: PS-PPO reduces critic-free RLHF compute and memory by updating sampled prefixes with importance weights that preserve an unbiased full-objective gradient estimate.

paragraphs: Reducing the precision of neural-network weights and activations saves computation, but intermediate partial sums can still consume substantial energy when accumulated at high precision. This paper targets that remaining cost in tiled accelerator architectures. Its analysis finds that extreme partial-sum values within a tile depend on the input.

PsumQuant uses post-training, input-aware quantization to predict partial-sum scales during inference. A learnable predictor uses the crest factor of input activations to account for extreme values while bounding the required bit-width. The scaling decision can therefore respond to the current input rather than rely solely on a fixed precision choice.

On a 128-by-128 systolic array, the method reduces partial sums to 8 bits with only a 1% accuracy drop on ResNet-18 and a 0.04 perplexity increase on Llama-3.1. The reported bit-width reduction produces a 45% reduction in total energy with minimal accuracy loss. These results identify accumulation precision as a practical source of further efficiency in NPU inference.
icml-2026-psumquant-in-line-post-trainin.tldr: PsumQuant dynamically scales intermediate partial sums, enabling 8-bit accumulation precision and a reported 45% total energy reduction with small quality losses.

paragraphs: A single success-or-failure reward gives a language model little information about which parts of an attempt caused the outcome. Yet code execution and other verifiable environments often provide explanations, such as runtime errors or judge feedback. This paper develops reinforcement learning that uses those richer signals.

Self-Distillation Policy Optimization conditions the current model on feedback and treats its resulting next-token predictions as a self-teacher. Those feedback-informed predictions are distilled back into the policy, creating a dense learning signal without an external teacher or explicit reward model. The method uses the model's ability to recognize mistakes retrospectively.

Experiments in scientific reasoning, tool use, and competitive programming show better sample efficiency and final accuracy than strong RLVR baselines. In scalar-only environments, successful rollouts provide implicit feedback for failed attempts, also improving results. Applied to individual questions at test time, SDPO reaches the same discovery probability as best-of-k sampling or multi-turn conversations with three times fewer attempts on difficult binary-reward tasks.
icml-2026-reinforcement-learning-via-sel.tldr: SDPO turns feedback-informed predictions from the model itself into dense training signals, improving learning efficiency and accuracy in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Scaling has improved many generative models, but its role in adversarial learning remains less explored. This paper investigates GANs that operate in a compact Variational Autoencoder latent space and use transformers for both the generator and discriminator. The combination is computationally efficient and supports scaling with more compute.

Simply enlarging the models exposes two problems: early generator layers are underused, and optimization becomes increasingly unstable. The authors address these with lightweight supervision at intermediate stages and learning-rate adjustments that account for model width. These changes target how the larger networks are trained, alongside the choice of representation and architecture.

The resulting Generative Adversarial Transformers train reliably from small to extra-large sizes. On class-conditional ImageNet generation at 256-by-256 resolution, GAT-XL achieves a reported state-of-the-art single-step FID of 2.18 in 60 epochs, using four times fewer epochs than strong baselines. The findings show that addressing layer utilization and optimization instability can make transformer-based adversarial generation scale effectively.
icml-2026-scalable-gans-with-transformer.tldr: Latent-space transformer GANs scale reliably after targeted training fixes, reaching a reported single-step ImageNet FID of 2.18 in 60 epochs.

paragraphs: Simulation can produce robot-training videos cheaply and in parallel, but their appearance and limited environmental variety can hinder real-world generalization. This paper introduces a video augmentation pipeline that converts simulated vision-language-action data into realistic videos while preserving the task meaning and action trajectories.

The pipeline extracts conditions through video semantic segmentation and captioning, rewrites captions to vary environments, and generates realistic videos with a conditional transfer model. Two additions make the process more economical: diffusion feature reuse shares video tokens across adjacent timesteps, and coreset sampling selects a compact, non-redundant subset to augment when computation is limited.

Experiments on Robotwin 2.0, LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and a real robotic platform show consistent improvements. Reported examples include an 8% improvement for RDT-1B on Robotwin 2.0 and a 5.1% improvement for pi_0 on LIBERO-Plus. The contribution combines visual realism and environmental diversity with mechanisms that reduce augmentation cost, making simulation-derived training data more useful in the evaluated robot-learning settings.
icml-2026-seeing-realism-from-simulation.tldr: The framework converts simulated robot videos into realistic, diverse training data while preserving actions and reducing augmentation cost.

paragraphs: An image can look convincing while containing the wrong number of parts or incorrect attachments. Shape-of-Thought addresses these structural failures by training a model to build objects progressively in rendered two-dimensional images. Each assembly decision is connected to an intermediate visual state that can be inspected.

A unified multimodal autoregressive model generates alternating textual plans and rendered states. It learns from supervision over the assembly process without producing explicit geometric representations or requiring external engines at inference. The authors introduce SoT-26K, a dataset of grounded traces derived from part-based CAD hierarchies, and T2S-CompBench to evaluate structural integrity and trace faithfulness.

After fine-tuning, the model reaches 88.4% on component numeracy and 84.8% on structural topology. These exceed direct generation by 24.2 and 19.3 percentage points, respectively. The intermediate images also make counts, connections, and part-addition errors visible along the trajectory. The results support progressive visual assembly as a way to improve structural generation while exposing the process for inspection.
icml-2026-shape-of-thought-progressive-o.tldr: Shape-of-Thought improves object counts and structural topology by generating inspectable visual assembly steps interleaved with textual plans.

paragraphs: Asset-allocation systems often forecast market behavior first and optimize a portfolio afterward. The authors argue that this separation creates a mismatch: reducing forecast error does not necessarily produce a robust portfolio. Their Signature-Informed Transformer combines feature extraction and allocation decisions within a single policy.

The model uses path signatures to encode dependencies in how asset trajectories evolve. A specialized attention mechanism targets geometric relationships among assets, and training directly minimizes Conditional Value at Risk, a measure focused on unfavorable outcomes. This makes the optimization objective explicitly reflect portfolio risk instead of relying on forecasting accuracy as an intermediate target.

The authors prove that their attention module amplifies signature-derived signals. Experiments across diverse equity universes show significant improvements over traditional strategies and advanced forecasting baselines. The contribution therefore connects a trajectory representation, a tailored attention mechanism, and a risk-aligned learning objective. Its empirical findings support the proposed integration of representation learning and portfolio decisions in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-signature-informed-transformer.tldr: A transformer combines path-signature features with direct portfolio-risk optimization, outperforming the evaluated traditional and forecasting-based allocation methods.

paragraphs: A representation can encode an ordered attribute along a direction, allowing examples to be ranked by where they fall on that axis. Prior work recovers such directions in vision encoders with very few labeled images, but text-only directions in vision-language models remain suboptimal. This paper examines whether multimodal language models offer a better language interface.

The authors hypothesize three possible advantages: ordinal understanding, embeddings that depend on conditioning, and a smaller gap between text and other modalities. They show that text prompts alone can reveal ranking directions in multimodal language-model embeddings, enabling zero-shot ranking without labeled examples to define the axis.

In the experiments, text-derived directions achieve 90% of the performance of supervised linear ranking directions, compared with 61% for vision-language-model embeddings. These figures describe relative performance, not absolute ranking accuracy. The analysis attributes the capability to conditional embeddings and a smaller modality gap, and demonstrates extension to audio. The findings suggest that language can directly probe ordered structure already present in multimodal representations.
icml-2026-zero-shot-rankability-revealin.tldr: Text prompts reveal ranking directions in multimodal language-model embeddings that reach 90% of supervised-axis performance in the reported experiments.
